recent_posts.title: Expanding visual search for online art collections
recent_posts.summary: A graduation research project combined Meta's DINOv2 embedding model and Segment Anything Model (SAM) to enable visual search across the Rijksmuseum's 800,000+ artwork collection. The prototype allows users to find similar artworks through image-to-image search and segment-based search, where specific details within paintings can be selected to discover visual connections across the collection. Embeddings were stored in Qdrant vector database using cosine similarity for nearest neighbor search. The segmented search processed 18,000 artworks, converting SAM's COCO_RLE masks into SVG polygons for interactive browser display. While promising, scaling challenges remain: processing the full collection would take 80 days with current infrastructure, and storing all segments would create a 25 million point vector database.

recent_posts.title: Why we love multiplatform with Kotlin and Compose
recent_posts.summary: Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) and Compose Multiplatform (CMP) enable sharing business logic and UI code across Android, iOS, web, and desktop while maintaining native performance. KMP allows writing data and business logic once and compiling it to native binaries for each platform, while CMP extends this to shared UI using declarative Compose syntax. Q42 uses KMP in production apps like McDonald's (serving millions across 60+ countries) to eliminate code duplication, reduce bugs, and speed up development. Unlike React Native's JavaScript runtime bridge, KMP compiles to native code with no translation layer, offering better performance and type safety. Teams can choose to share only logic (using native SwiftUI/Compose for UI) or share both logic and UI with CMP, maintaining flexibility for platform-specific customizations when needed.

recent_posts.title: Building an accessible 3D website for discovering mobility aids
recent_posts.summary: A frontend developer with cerebral palsy shares the journey of building To Come Home, a 3D interactive website that helps young disabled people discover mobility aids. The project uses a house metaphor with room-based navigation, built with React, ThreeJS, and Blender, where users can explore hotspots tied to daily activities. Unlike traditional medical supply sites that target caregivers or seniors, this platform is user-powered, allowing disabled individuals to recommend tools themselves. The developer conducted extensive user research with a test panel of young disabled adults and medical professionals to ensure the design respected their capabilities rather than patronizing them.

recent_posts.title: Searching through museum collections
recent_posts.summary: Q42 built a new search and recommendation system for Rijksmuseum's online collection, combining Elasticsearch for full-text search with Neo4j graph database for relationship-based browsing. The system transforms linked data from multiple museum collections (art, library, archive) into a unified model that enables faceted search, node-based exploration, and contextual recommendations. Key technical challenges included mapping complex SPARQL queries to simplified data models, handling densely connected nodes in the graph, and balancing performance between the two database systems. After launch, the team shifted more search functionality to Elasticsearch while keeping Neo4j for relationship-heavy tasks like generating node pages and recommendations.

recent_posts.title: Making wildlife cameras smart with embedded AI
recent_posts.summary: A developer with no embedded experience successfully created a custom AI module for wildlife cameras using the Seeed Studio Grove Vision AI module. The project involved reverse engineering firmware, training custom hippo detection models, and implementing a communication protocol to achieve 99.16% detection accuracy with sub-second response times. The solution addresses power consumption and speed limitations of previous cloud-based systems, enabling real-time wildlife detection for conservation efforts.

recent_posts.title: Building scalable AR experiences for museums using Cloud Anchors and image recognition
recent_posts.summary: A developer at Q42 created an AR solution for the Rijksmuseum that allows staff to create and manage AR content at scale. The project combined Google Cloud Anchors with image recognition to overcome AR's inherent limitations, achieving high precision (within 5mm) while enabling content creation outside gallery hours. The solution uses reference points and averaging algorithms to handle tracking jitter, making AR experiences maintainable even with changing museum environments.

recent_posts.title: Transitioning to SwiftUI with Server Driven UI
recent_posts.summary: SwiftUI has revolutionized UI development since its introduction in 2019. The HEMA app, developed by Q42, recently transitioned from UIKit to SwiftUI, leveraging Server Driven UI for improved efficiency and developer satisfaction. Despite initial challenges, the team successfully implemented the transition, enhanced collaboration with the design team, and significantly accelerated development speed. The post highlights the team's journey, including technical strategies and the benefits realized.

recent_posts.title: Using AI to analyse politician's speeches in real time
recent_posts.summary: A team of software engineers created a prototype AI system called Klartext to analyze political speeches in real-time at Sweden's Almedalsveckan. They faced challenges like live speech transcription and prompt engineering for Large Language Models. Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) such as promise tracking and emotional vs. rational scoring were measured. The system's back-end was built to scale using Firebase's cloud functions and maintained real-time updates through Firestore. The prototype successfully transitioned to a production-ready state, providing insightful real-time analysis during the event.

recent_posts.title: Revolutionising the way art collections are presented online
recent_posts.summary: A tech agency and design partner have built an interactive and immersive web experience called Oculi Mundi to showcase The Sunderland Collection. The website pushes the limits of design patterns, innovation, and technology to create a highly immersive and engaging experience. Challenges included 3D rendering technologies, accessibility, and creating a unique user interface.
